name: LGBTQ movements
summary: LGBTQ movements are the campaigns for the equal rights and dignity of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer people. Britannica describes a civil rights movement seeking an end to sodomy laws and to discrimination in employment, housing and public life, and later military service, hate crimes protection, marriage rights and action on HIV/AIDS. Scholarship describes a guiding ideology that swings between assimilation into mainstream institutions and liberation from sexism and the gender-role system.
scope: The movement for lesbian and gay rights and its later bisexual, transgender and queer extensions, as Britannica's account of the gay rights movement and Engel's scholarly history define it, with the homophile organisations (Mattachine) as its origin and the Stonewall riots as its turning point. Both poles Engel names count: the assimilationist, civil-rights strand and the liberationist strand of the Gay Liberation Front and Wittman's manifesto. It excludes queer theory as an academic field, LGBTQ conservatism and the positions of single organisations beyond what these sources tie to the movement, and it answers a statement only where these sources settle it.

aliases.name: LGBT movement
aliases.quote: The gay rights movement , or LGBT movement refers to myriad organizations, groups, and people broadly fighting for the rights of lesbian , gay , bisexual , and transgendered people (LGBT).

sources.title: Gay rights movement, Britannica
sources.author: Michael Levy and the Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.usedFor: Defines the movement and lists its aims: equal rights, repeal of sodomy laws, an end to discrimination, military service, hate crimes law, marriage rights and AIDS policy.

sources.title: Tracing the rainbow: an historical sketch of the American gay and lesbian movement, in The Unfinished Revolution (Engel), Cambridge University Press, chapter 2

sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of the movement's guiding ideology as a swing between assimilationism and liberationism, and of its campaigns on the military ban, employment law, hate crimes and AIDS.

notes: Themes searched, with nothing settled on the lines the validator names (pluralism and authoritarianism, class, the economy, secularism, racial equality, centralism, monarchy, nationalism, foreign policy, the environment): the saved texts hold no stated position there beyond Wittman saying the movement has not worked out an economic system and Engel noting the Christian right as an opponent. Other themes searched: the movement's definition and history (Britannica, Engel), liberationist texts (Wittman; the UK Gay Liberation Front manifesto and Queers Read This were read but not cited because no defining source ties them to the movement by title), the Yogyakarta Principles and the UN human rights office page. Only seven statements are settled by sources that define the movement; most statements, including economic, ecological and foreign policy ones, are not addressed, and the two strands Engel describes differ on marriage, the family and tactics. The Yogyakarta Principles were not cited because no defining source ties them to the movement. No missing statement met the rule of two quotes from separate cited places. The movement is plural, so an answer rests on the aims both strands share or on the one strand that speaks.
